flashcards.front: If 1 page request fans out in parallel to K=20 backend shards with p99 = 40ms each, what % of page loads hit >40ms tail latency?
flashcards.back: `1 - (0.99)^20 = ~18.2%`! Parallel scatter-gather fan-out amplifies tail-latency impact linearly with fan-out factor unless mitigated by hedged requests and shard deadlines.

flashcards.front: How does Shuffle Sharding improve multi-tenant blast radius isolation over standard partitioning?
flashcards.back: Mapping each tenant to a random subset of K=2 cells out of M=16 pools yields 120 virtual combinations (`M choose K`), ensuring a single toxic tenant saturates <8% of overlap with healthy customers.

quizzes.scenario: Your gateway fans every dashboard call out to 25 services in parallel. Each has a p99 of 45 ms.
quizzes.question: Roughly what share of dashboard calls exceed 45 ms, and what reduces it?
options: About 1%, since each service is slow only 1% of the time
About 22%; add deadlines and hedge idempotent calls past p95
About 22%; lowering every timeout to 45 ms removes it
About 25%; adding more replicas per service removes it
quizzes.explanation: A call is slow if any of the 25 parallel calls is slow: 1 - 0.99^25 is about 22%. Per-call deadlines and hedged requests (sending a second copy of idempotent calls after roughly the p95 latency, within a retry budget) cut the tail.
optionExplanations: That ignores that any one of 25 slow calls slows the whole request.
Hard 45 ms timeouts turn slow calls into errors instead of answers.
The estimate is close, but replicas alone do not cut tail latency.

quizzes.scenario: A traffic spike triples gateway ingress from 500k to 1.5M requests per second, and downstream queues grow past their delay target.
quizzes.question: What protects the p99 of high-priority traffic?
options: Queue every request until downstream capacity catches up
Retry failed requests immediately at the gateway
Shed low-priority requests early with 429 and a jittered retry
Raise downstream timeouts so fewer requests fail outright
quizzes.explanation: Once demand exceeds capacity, queues only add delay. Shed low-priority requests early with 429 and Retry-After (with jitter), using queue delay (as in CoDel) or concurrency limits from Little's Law to decide when, so admitted requests still meet the SLA.
optionExplanations: Long queues mean every request misses its deadline.
Immediate retries add load at the worst possible moment.
Correct. Admitted traffic stays inside the latency target.
Longer timeouts hold more resources and slow recovery.
